HOW TO COMPARE
Every screen shows the same moment: Spring 1867, season 5 of 20. The post has just arrived — the Weekly reports McCoy buying every board in Abilene, the saloon says a county railroad-bond vote is coming, church talk puts Texas longhorns at $4 a head. Same ledger everywhere: cash $41.50, store tab $28 at 3%/month, cellar ¾, three visits left.

Row 1: the three the group picked from round one. Row 2: five new directions in the same territory — period, illustrated, unmistakably a game — each borrowing a proven pattern from a best-in-class educational or narrative game.

Ask of each: Does it read as a game or a lesson? Does information feel like something you go looking for? Does wealth visibly change what you see? Would an 18–25 year old open it on the bus?

A · PLAT MAP — ink on paper, the county as the hub
Motivation: the town is the canary. You literally watch the surveyor's stakes go in and the stockyard appear. Information lives in places you choose to visit.
Tradeoff: a map of squares is quiet. Needs strong scenes inside the buildings to carry emotion.

B · STORYBOOK — painted scenes, narrative first
Motivation: the most emotional read. Choices are people, not tickers. Closest to 80 Days / Reigns, which the audience already knows.
Tradeoff: money can feel like something that happens to you rather than something you manage. Weakest at showing a portfolio.

C · PIXEL FRONTIER — retro pixel art, dialog box, menu
Motivation: instantly reads as a game, and as Oregon Trail specifically — the positioning in one screenshot. Cheapest art pipeline.
Tradeoff: nostalgia may read as a joke to some of the audience; hard to make ledger numbers feel serious in a pixel font.

F · JOURNAL — your own handwritten account book
Pattern: Pentiment's manuscript world; the ledger as the literacy artifact. Every season is a page you wrote; the debrief is re-reading your own entries. The numbers live in Dr./Cr. columns the player fills.
Motivation: the most personal and the most honest about money — it's your handwriting, your arithmetic. Naturally becomes the 'letters home.'
Tradeoff: script faces strain legibility on a phone; slow, quiet pace may lose players who want a game to feel like a game.

G · POSTER — flat WPA / national-park poster art
Pattern: Firewatch's poster look with Duolingo-grade clarity — big type, big targets, a segmented progress bar you can read at arm's length.
Motivation: the most legible and the most shareable; screenshots look like posters. Best for accessibility and for onboarding an audience that doesn't play strategy games.
Tradeoff: bold flat art can feel generic if the illustration isn't excellent; less room for information density (the post is one line here).

H · DECK — swipe cards with engraved portraits
Pattern: Reigns. One card, one decision, one thumb. Four house meters (cash, debt, cellar, standing) shift with every swipe, so tradeoffs are visible before you commit.
Motivation: the most mobile-native loop; sessions are seconds long; the meters teach 'every choice moves four things' without a word of explanation.
Tradeoff: binary swipes flatten investing into yes/no — sizing, structure, and 'how much' need a third gesture (the hold button here). Cards can feel arbitrary if history isn't foregrounded.

I · DIORAMA — your claim as a small isometric world
Pattern: Monument Valley / Townscaper. The diorama is the progress bar: sod house becomes frame house becomes barn; the rail grade's stakes appear at the edge; a pin marks the deal in town.
Motivation: 'money makes your world expand' made literal — the transcript's own line. Watching it compound is the reward, which is exactly the behavior we want to make satisfying.
Tradeoff: the most expensive art pipeline (every asset in every state); risks reading as a cozy farm game rather than a finance game.

J · PANELS — the season as a graphic-novel page
Pattern: Overboard / Framed. Events read left to right in panels; the player's choice fills the last one. Two-tone ink with one spot color.
Motivation: panels teach sequence and cause-and-effect by their shape. The Almanac debrief becomes 'the strip that actually happened' laid next to yours. Cheap to produce per scene; huge range of tone.
Tradeoff: text-heavy; the ledger is a footer, not a mechanic; some readers skip panels the way they skip cutscenes.

D · BROADSHEET — set aside after round one
The newspaper as interface. Kept here for reference; the information-as-headline idea may still belong inside another direction's newspaper office.

E · TICKERTAPE — set aside after round one
Contemporary fintech chrome. Kept for reference; the reliability bars on each signal are worth stealing for whichever direction wins.
